title: OPP: We had no other choice
article: Ontario Provincial Police officers could not have done anything differently on the night they shot and killed a driver who was ramming their cruisers in a desperate attempt to escape, two officers involved in the tragic incident told a coroner's inquest Monday.

"That night, things unfolded as they did. We were strictly in a reaction mode. We could not get it to go any other way," OPP Const. Aftim Nassar told day one of the inquest into the July 2009 death of Phillip Jeffrey Charbonneau.
Nassar added his colleagues were in shock in the moments after the shots were fired and they realized Charbonneau was dead.
"This is not what anybody wants," said Nassar.
"We all want to go home at the end of the day."
Charbonneau, 35, died in a confrontation with police at Forthton on the night of Friday, July 3, 2009.

The Special Investigations Unit (SIU), a civilian agency that investigates deaths or serious injuries involving police, later that year cleared the two subject officers they investigated in the incident, saying they reasonably believed their lives were in danger.
Coroner Dr. David Evans is presiding over the inquest, which includes a jury of four women and one man.
It is expected to last 10 days and hear from 22 witnesses.

In his instructions to the jury, Evans stressed the purpose of the inquest is not a finding of guilt, but a finding of fact to determine whether anything can be done to prevent such a tragedy from happening again.

Nassar and OPP Const. Rob Sinclair both described an incident that began with Charbonneau's black pickup truck pulling up to a Reduce Impaired Driving Everywhere (RIDE) check on the westbound Highway 401 off-ramp in Brockville.
At 11:02 p.m. that day, Nassar said he stopped Charbonneau, who was alone in the vehicle, smelled alcohol on his breath and noticed signs of agitation from Charbonneau that resembled flu symptoms.
"He seemed extremely nervous," Nassar told the inquest.
"He was sweaty. He was very clammy-looking."
"His mouth was open. His eyes were wide."
When Nassar "called him" on the issue of alcohol, the constable said, Charbonneau began stuttering and looking around him "like he was trying to run."
When Nassar told Charbonneau to pull over to the shoulder of the on-ramp, the driver made as if to do so, but then took off, prompting a chase.
Charbonneau tore through Brockville and sped north, said Nassar, reaching 150 km/h before leaving the city's north end and hitting speeds of 180 on County Road 29.

OPP officers out of the Leeds County detachment office in Spring Valley set up at Murray Road, where they deployed a spike belt, but that did not stop the driver, so police decided to use a "rolling block," a tactic used to slow a vehicle down by surrounding it on all sides.

The runaway driver went around one vehicle at the intersection of Centennial Road before leaving Brockville, then, after the spike belt was deployed, when he reached Foster Hall Road, he swerved -- deliberately -- into the southbound lane in an attempt to collide with an oncoming vehicle, the testifying officers said.
The second driver avoided the collision by veering off the road, they added.

Sgt. Jason Butcher, driving a police SUV, got in front of Charbonneau's truck, which by now was slowing down and losing its front tires as a result of the spike belt, and another OPP cruiser, driven by Const. Mike Benn also got in front, said Sinclair.
Both officers described Charbonneau ramming the vehicles in front of him to try to escape.

Among the discrepancies in their separate accounts was the speed of the chase, with Sinclair saying Charbonneau went up to 140 km/h in Brockville, and their version of a particularly rough collision, north of the OPP station, between Charbonneau's pickup truck and the police vehicles now in front of him.
"I saw the back end of the pickup truck raise off the ground," said Nassar, adding the truck went up so high, he could see its undercarriage up to the front wheels.
Sinclair, who was closer to that collision, said it was Butcher's police SUV that buckled up to that extent.

The pickup truck finally came to a stop in front of the Cedar Valley Golf Club, near the County Road 42 turnoff at Forthton, the officers said, but Charbonneau then began ramming the vehicles in front of and behind him in an attempt to create a gap and escape.

Sinclair, who managed to smash the pickup's driver's side window with his baton, said his foot was run over just before that in Charbonneau's back-and-forth ramming and he ultimately pulled out his firearm.
Another officer, Const. Brian Jones, was standing beside him and also had his gun out.

Sinclair said he distinctly heard Butcher and Jones warn that they would shoot if Charbonneau did not stop, and said he had his own gun out because he feared Charbonneau would run over his colleagues.
Neither officer mentioned who opened fire.
Nassar was heading back to his vehicle when the shooting began, while Sinclair said he heard one shot followed by four others in rapid succession: "Pop, pop-pop-pop-pop."
Both constables said they knew Charbonneau was dead as soon as they saw him.
According to Nassar, Butcher had a look of disbelief on his face, while Const. Jones appeared to be in shock.
Reading from his notes, Nassar said Jones said: "Oh my God.
He was going to kill me.
I can't believe it."
Sinclair said he did not believe the officers could have done anything differently and both the pursuit and the firearm discharge were done according to proper procedures.

Lawrence Greenspon, the lawyer for Charbonneau's family, challenged the officers on discrepancies between their testimonies Monday and interviews they gave shortly after the incident to the SIU and OPP.
In particular, he told Nassar there was nothing in those interviews or his duty notes suggesting Charbonneau had his mouth open and eyes wide back at the RIDE checkpoint.
"When did it come to you, this new and improved, new and embellished description of Mr. Charbonneau?" asked Greenspon.
"When I close my eyes and think about it, I see it," replied Nassar.

Greenspon also questioned Nassar's description of the dead shooting victim with his hands on his lap, suggesting the officer added that detail in after another eyewitness told the media she saw Charbonneau's hands in the "10 to two" position on his steering wheel after the shooting.
Nassar vehemently rejected the suggestion, saying he never saw that media account.
Charbonneau's two teenage daughters sat with other loved ones in the audience and began crying when Nassar first described finding their father dead.
Jessica Monette, Charbonneau's common-law partner for seven years, was the first on the stand, tearfully recalling how she learned the morning after that he was dead.
Charbonneau's driver's licence had been suspended because of previously unpaid speeding tickets, she said.
"He knew he was guilty of them, just we were on a very limited budget and it was hard to pay," said Monette.
On at least one occasion in the past, when he was driving, he panicked at the sight of a police cruiser appearing to turn to follow them, she said.
Under questioning by coroner's counsel Robert Wadden, Monette said Charbonneau had suffered from an addiction previously in their relationship and might have relapsed.
She also said it was unusual for him not to have come home that Friday night.
The inquest continues today at the Brockville courthouse.
